evidenceSummary : Consensus statement from an international Panther Symposium group of 26 ACL experts (surgeons, sports medicine physicians, physical therapists and scientists), built by a modified Delphi process with an 80% agreement threshold and a MEDLINE literature review. Of 11 statements, consensus was reached that return to sport means regaining the preinjury level of sport, that purely time-based decisions should be abandoned (26 of 26), and that decisions need objective examination data (26 of 26), a validated test (23 of 26) and a validated psychological readiness measure (22 of 26). Coach involvement in the clearance decision did not reach consensus (7 of 26).
screeningLimitations : The statements are expert opinion built on a single MEDLINE search covering 5 to 10 years, and the authors did not use a formal systematic review. The authors state that the ideal test battery, psychological tools and biological healing measures remain unresolved.
synthesisCaution : Staff could read the statements as a validated return-to-sport protocol with fixed criteria, when the authors describe them as consensus principles and say the exact test battery and thresholds still need research.
year : 2020
citation : Meredith SJ, Rauer T, Chmielewski TL, et al. Return to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: Panther Symposium ACL Injury Return to Sport Consensus Group. Orthop J Sports Med 2020;8(6):2325967120930829.
doi : 10.1177/2325967120930829
abstract : Background: a precise and consistent definition of return to sport (RTS) after ACL injury is lacking. Purpose: to define RTS, describe the RTS continuum and give guidance on RTS testing and decisions. Study design: consensus statement. Methods: an international multidisciplinary group used a modified Delphi method, with a literature review. Results: RTS is achieved when the preinjury level of sport is reached, through criteria-based progression from return to participation to RTS and return to performance. Purely time-based decisions should be abandoned; decisions should be made by a multidisciplinary group using objective examination data and validated, peer-reviewed RTS tests that include functional and psychological assessment, and should consider biological healing, context and concomitant injuries. Conclusion: research is needed on the ideal test battery, psychological readiness testing and biological assessment of healing.
tldr : Return to sport after ACL injury should mean regaining the preinjury level of sport, reached through criteria-based stages. Time alone should not decide clearance, and the decision should use examination data, validated tests and psychological readiness.
methods : International consensus group of 26 ACL experts convened at a symposium in June 2019. A modified Delphi process ran three rounds (internet survey, structured in-person discussion and a final vote), with 80% agreement set in advance as consensus. Two liaisons completed a MEDLINE search (June 2019; anterior cruciate ligament, return to sport and return to play; 5 to 10 years) to support the statements.
findings : Consensus was reached on 11 statements. Return to sport was defined as the preinjury level of sport (24 of 26, 92%), and purely time-based decisions should be abandoned (26 of 26). Objective physical examination was required (26 of 26), with validated tests (23 of 26) and a validated psychological readiness scale (22 of 26). Cited data from the Delaware-Oslo cohort show that patients who passed a criteria-based test at 6 months returned to their previous level at 81% (1 year) and 84% (2 years).
limitations : The statements are consensus opinion built from an expert panel and a single MEDLINE search, not a systematic review or meta-analysis. The authors note that the best test battery, the psychological tools to use, and how to assess biological healing are not yet known. Some statements, such as the role of the coach, did not reach consensus, and the cited RTS outcomes come mainly from one cohort.
practicalImplications : Use criteria-based progression through return to participation, return to sport and return to performance, with a documented clearance by the health care provider before unrestricted training. Include objective examination, a validated test battery and a psychological readiness measure, and consider contextual factors such as position, sport and concomitant injury. Avoid clearing an athlete on time alone, and treat RTS before about 6 months as likely high risk.
athleteDev : Apply the RTS continuum to sport-specific training: clear unrestricted training first, then full participation in practice, then competition, with serial testing at each stage. Measure readiness with objective tests of strength, hop and movement quality before progressing, and do not use the calendar as the trigger.
rtp : The statements describe a criteria-based return to sport after ACL injury, requiring objective examination, a validated test battery and psychological readiness, with time used as a guide to graft healing rather than the decision. The paper cannot specify the exact test battery or thresholds, and it cannot be used as a validated clearance protocol or as a guarantee of return to the preinjury level.

Background: A precise and consistent definition of return to sport (RTS) after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury is lacking, and
there is controversy surrounding the process of returning patients to sport and their previous activity level.
Purpose: The aim of the Panther Symposium ACL Injury Return to Sport Consensus Group was to provide a clear definition of RTS
after ACL injury and a description of the RTS continuum as well as provide clinical guidance on RTS testing and decision-making.
Study Design: Consensus statement.
Methods: An international, multidisciplinary group of ACL experts convened as part of a consensus meeting. Consensus
statements were developed using a modified Delphi method. Literature review was performed to report the supporting
evidence.
Results: Key points include that RTS is characterized by achievement of the preinjury level of sport and involves a criteria-based
progression from return to participation to RTS and, ultimately, return to performance. Purely time-based RTS decision-making
should be abandoned. Progression occurs along an RTS continuum, with decision-making by a multidisciplinary group that
incorporates objective physical examination data and validated and peer-reviewed RTS tests, which should involve functional
assessment as well as psychological readiness. Consideration should be given to biological healing, contextual factors, and
concomitant injuries.
Conclusion: The resultant consensus statements and scientific rationale aim to inform the reader of the complex process
of RTS after ACL injury that occurs along a dynamic continuum. Research is needed to determine the ideal RTS test
battery, the best implementation of psychological readiness testing, and methods for the biological assessment of healing
and recovery.

evidenceSummary : Consensus statement from an international Panther Symposium group of 26 ACL experts (surgeons, sports medicine physicians, physical therapists and scientists), built by a modified Delphi process with an 80% agreement threshold and a MEDLINE literature review. Of 11 statements, consensus was reached that return to sport means regaining the preinjury level of sport, that purely time-based decisions should be abandoned (26 of 26), and that decisions need objective examination data (26 of 26), a validated test (23 of 26) and a validated psychological readiness measure (22 of 26). Coach involvement in the clearance decision did not reach consensus (7 of 26).
screeningLimitations : The statements are expert opinion built on a single MEDLINE search covering 5 to 10 years, and the authors did not use a formal systematic review. The authors state that the ideal test battery, psychological tools and biological healing measures remain unresolved.
synthesisCaution : Staff could read the statements as a validated return-to-sport protocol with fixed criteria, when the authors describe them as consensus principles and say the exact test battery and thresholds still need research.
year : 2020
citation : Meredith SJ, Rauer T, Chmielewski TL, et al. Return to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: Panther Symposium ACL Injury Return to Sport Consensus Group. Orthop J Sports Med 2020;8(6):2325967120930829.
doi : 10.1177/2325967120930829
abstract : Background: a precise and consistent definition of return to sport (RTS) after ACL injury is lacking. Purpose: to define RTS, describe the RTS continuum and give guidance on RTS testing and decisions. Study design: consensus statement. Methods: an international multidisciplinary group used a modified Delphi method, with a literature review. Results: RTS is achieved when the preinjury level of sport is reached, through criteria-based progression from return to participation to RTS and return to performance. Purely time-based decisions should be abandoned; decisions should be made by a multidisciplinary group using objective examination data and validated, peer-reviewed RTS tests that include functional and psychological assessment, and should consider biological healing, context and concomitant injuries. Conclusion: research is needed on the ideal test battery, psychological readiness testing and biological assessment of healing.
tldr : Return to sport after ACL injury should mean regaining the preinjury level of sport, reached through criteria-based stages. Time alone should not decide clearance, and the decision should use examination data, validated tests and psychological readiness.
methods : International consensus group of 26 ACL experts convened at a symposium in June 2019. A modified Delphi process ran three rounds (internet survey, structured in-person discussion and a final vote), with 80% agreement set in advance as consensus. Two liaisons completed a MEDLINE search (June 2019; anterior cruciate ligament, return to sport and return to play; 5 to 10 years) to support the statements.
findings : Consensus was reached on 11 statements. Return to sport was defined as the preinjury level of sport (24 of 26, 92%), and purely time-based decisions should be abandoned (26 of 26). Objective physical examination was required (26 of 26), with validated tests (23 of 26) and a validated psychological readiness scale (22 of 26). Cited data from the Delaware-Oslo cohort show that patients who passed a criteria-based test at 6 months returned to their previous level at 81% (1 year) and 84% (2 years).
limitations : The statements are consensus opinion built from an expert panel and a single MEDLINE search, not a systematic review or meta-analysis. The authors note that the best test battery, the psychological tools to use, and how to assess biological healing are not yet known. Some statements, such as the role of the coach, did not reach consensus, and the cited RTS outcomes come mainly from one cohort.
practicalImplications : Use criteria-based progression through return to participation, return to sport and return to performance, with a documented clearance by the health care provider before unrestricted training. Include objective examination, a validated test battery and a psychological readiness measure, and consider contextual factors such as position, sport and concomitant injury. Avoid clearing an athlete on time alone, and treat RTS before about 6 months as likely high risk.
athleteDev : Apply the RTS continuum to sport-specific training: clear unrestricted training first, then full participation in practice, then competition, with serial testing at each stage. Measure readiness with objective tests of strength, hop and movement quality before progressing, and do not use the calendar as the trigger.
rtp : The statements describe a criteria-based return to sport after ACL injury, requiring objective examination, a validated test battery and psychological readiness, with time used as a guide to graft healing rather than the decision. The paper cannot specify the exact test battery or thresholds, and it cannot be used as a validated clearance protocol or as a guarantee of return to the preinjury level.

Background: A precise and consistent definition of return to sport (RTS) after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury is lacking, and
there is controversy surrounding the process of returning patients to sport and their previous activity level.
Purpose: The aim of the Panther Symposium ACL Injury Return to Sport Consensus Group was to provide a clear definition of RTS
after ACL injury and a description of the RTS continuum as well as provide clinical guidance on RTS testing and decision-making.
Study Design: Consensus statement.
Methods: An international, multidisciplinary group of ACL experts convened as part of a consensus meeting. Consensus
statements were developed using a modified Delphi method. Literature review was performed to report the supporting
evidence.
Results: Key points include that RTS is characterized by achievement of the preinjury level of sport and involves a criteria-based
progression from return to participation to RTS and, ultimately, return to performance. Purely time-based RTS decision-making
should be abandoned. Progression occurs along an RTS continuum, with decision-making by a multidisciplinary group that
incorporates objective physical examination data and validated and peer-reviewed RTS tests, which should involve functional
assessment as well as psychological readiness. Consideration should be given to biological healing, contextual factors, and
concomitant injuries.
Conclusion: The resultant consensus statements and scientific rationale aim to inform the reader of the complex process
of RTS after ACL injury that occurs along a dynamic continuum. Research is needed to determine the ideal RTS test
battery, the best implementation of psychological readiness testing, and methods for the biological assessment of healing
and recovery.

evidenceSummary : Single case report of a 23-year-old male elite football player with a grade 2c intramuscular tendon hamstring injury sustained in an English Premier League match. Rehabilitation used the control-chaos continuum, with isometric posterior chain force testing, ultrasound and GPS load monitoring. The player returned to on-pitch rehabilitation at 11 days, full team training at 35 days, and played 40 days after injury, with no reinjury for the rest of the season.
screeningLimitations : This is one player in one club, with no comparison group, so the findings cannot show that the monitoring or loading approach causes a faster or safer return. The authors state that the timeline and responses are player-specific and may not transfer to other footballers.
synthesisCaution : Staff could read the 35-day return to full training or the 40-day return to play as a benchmark for intramuscular tendon injuries, when they describe one player whose timeline depends on his injury, club context and coaching decisions.
year : 2022
citation : Taberner M, O'Keefe J, Dunn A, Cohen DD. Return to sport and beyond following intramuscular tendon hamstring injury: A case report of an English Premier League football player. Physical Therapy in Sport 2022;56:38-47.
doi : 10.1016/j.ptsp.2022.05.013
abstract : Background: hamstring strains are the most common injury in elite football and carry a high reinjury risk, especially when the intramuscular tendon (IMT) is involved, and rehabilitation data for these injuries are limited. Case scenario: an elite player suffered a grade 2c hamstring injury in an EPL match and was managed with early care, progressive off-pitch physical preparation and the control-chaos continuum for on-pitch rehabilitation, with objective and subjective load-response monitoring. Outcomes: on-pitch rehabilitation at 11 days, full team training at 35 days, match play at 40 days, and no reinjury for the rest of the season. Conclusion: knowledge of the IMT and expected return timeframes, with performance and load-response monitoring, communication and practitioner experience, may help to guide return to sport.
tldr : A single elite player with an intramuscular tendon hamstring injury returned to full team training at 35 days and played at 40 days without reinjury. Isometric strength monitoring and load tracking guided each step, but this is one case.
methods : Single case report of one 23-year-old male player managed by the club's medical and sports science staff. Care followed a modified return-to-sport continuum with the control-chaos continuum for on-pitch work. Isometric posterior chain peak force (unilateral test on a force platform at 1000 Hz) and interlimb asymmetry were measured weekly and before most training sessions. GPS load and MRI and ultrasound were used at set points, and the player gave informed consent.
findings : Interlimb asymmetry in isometric posterior chain peak force fell below 10% by day 11, and the player reached his pre-injury weekly running load before full team training at day 35. He then played as a substitute for about 40 to 45 minutes in five matches and started one 90-minute match, where his high-speed running was 1.26 times his typical pre-injury game load, with no reinjury for the rest of the season. Authors note that the largest force decline came about 48 hours after match play, and it was symmetrical across both limbs.
limitations : Findings come from one player, one club and one injury, without a control group or a validated threshold for IPC asymmetry. The authors state that the timeline and the monitoring approach may not transfer to other players or clubs, and that the link between the monitoring and reinjury risk is unproven.
practicalImplications : Use an isometric strength test and load data before each stage of return, and combine them with pain response and player feedback. Consider an early phase of controlled loading and partial team involvement, as the authors describe, but expect the timeline to vary by injury and player. Keep monitoring after return to play, since the authors judged the reinjury risk after this injury type to be high.
athleteDev : Use the control-chaos continuum to build back to match demands: progress high-speed running and maximal speed exposure against the match demand, and check strength asymmetry the morning after sessions. The case suggests that matching training volume to the player's pre-injury weekly running load was a practical target before full team training.
rtp : The case describes one player who returned to team training at 35 days and to match play at 40 days after an intramuscular tendon hamstring injury, without reinjury for the season. It cannot set a return-to-play timeline for this injury, because the authors recommend an individual approach and the case involves no comparison.

tldr : A single elite player with an intramuscular tendon hamstring injury returned to full team training at 35 days and played at 40 days without reinjury. Isometric strength monitoring and load tracking guided each step, but this is one case.
methods : Single case report of one 23-year-old male player managed by the club's medical and sports science staff. Care followed a modified return-to-sport continuum with the control-chaos continuum for on-pitch work. Isometric posterior chain peak force (unilateral test on a force platform at 1000 Hz) and interlimb asymmetry were measured weekly and before most training sessions. GPS load and MRI and ultrasound were used at set points, and the player gave informed consent.
findings : Interlimb asymmetry in isometric posterior chain peak force fell below 10% by day 11, and the player reached his pre-injury weekly running load before full team training at day 35. He then played as a substitute for about 40 to 45 minutes in five matches and started one 90-minute match, where his high-speed running was 1.26 times his typical pre-injury game load, with no reinjury for the rest of the season. Authors note that the largest force decline came about 48 hours after match play, and it was symmetrical across both limbs.
limitations : Findings come from one player, one club and one injury, without a control group or a validated threshold for IPC asymmetry. The authors state that the timeline and the monitoring approach may not transfer to other players or clubs, and that the link between the monitoring and reinjury risk is unproven.
practicalImplications : Use an isometric strength test and load data before each stage of return, and combine them with pain response and player feedback. Consider an early phase of controlled loading and partial team involvement, as the authors describe, but expect the timeline to vary by injury and player. Keep monitoring after return to play, since the authors judged the reinjury risk after this injury type to be high.
athleteDev : Use the control-chaos continuum to build back to match demands: progress high-speed running and maximal speed exposure against the match demand, and check strength asymmetry the morning after sessions. The case suggests that matching training volume to the player's pre-injury weekly running load was a practical target before full team training.
rtp : The case describes one player who returned to team training at 35 days and to match play at 40 days after an intramuscular tendon hamstring injury, without reinjury for the season. It cannot set a return-to-play timeline for this injury, because the authors recommend an individual approach and the case involves no comparison.

evidenceSummary : Narrative review of return to sport after distal biceps tendon repair in athletes, drawing on four studies: 10 weightlifters (D'Alessandro), 61 analysed athletes from mixed sports (Gowd), 35 NFL players (McGinnis) and 22 NFL players (Pagani). The authors report a pooled return to sport of 95.3%, a return to the same level of 81.8%, and a mean time to return of 38.8 weeks. No search method, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal is described.
screeningLimitations : The review draws on four small, mostly retrospective series with different sports, outcomes and rehabilitation protocols, and it reports no confounder adjustment. The pooled return rate cannot be reproduced from the per-study counts, so the evidence cannot set clearance criteria or an individual return timeline.
synthesisCaution : Staff could read the 95% return rate as a likely outcome for any athlete, when it comes from small series, mostly of NFL players and weightlifters, with no comparison group and a possible loss of athletes with complications.
year : 2023
citation : Wörner EA, Nagel M, Kodde IF, Eygendaal D, The B. Return to sports following distal biceps tendon repair: a current concepts review. Journal of ISAKOS 2023 (accepted pre-proof).
doi : 10.1016/j.jisako.2023.02.004
abstract : The article has no abstract in the pre-proof text. Its summary points state that distal biceps tendon repair has a high return-to-sports rate (95%), with 82% returning to the same preinjury level; that functional outcomes are good and not clinically different from matched athletes; that the time to return is long, about 40 weeks; and that the current literature is sparse.
tldr : Most athletes return to sport after distal biceps tendon repair, but usually to the same level only after about 39 weeks, so a return within the same season is unlikely in many sports. The evidence is small and retrospective, so timelines should be set with the athlete and coach.
methods : Narrative review of studies on return to sport after distal biceps tendon repair in athletes. The text does not describe a search strategy, databases, inclusion criteria or appraisal method. The included studies are summarised in a demographics table and a logistic regression table from one study.
findings : Return to sport was 100% (10 of 10) in the weightlifter series, 93.4% (57 of 61) in Gowd et al, 94% (33 of 35) in the NFL series by McGinnis et al (Table 1 gives 95%), and 84% (21 of 22) in Pagani et al. The authors report a mean return time of 6.0 months in Gowd et al and similar NFL performance scores to matched controls, but a shorter career length for defensive backs in Pagani et al. In Gowd et al, a single-incision approach and dominant-side surgery were associated with a longer time to return, and suture anchor fixation with a lower chance of returning at the same or higher level.
limitations : The review has no described search or appraisal, and it relies on four small retrospective studies with different outcomes, sports and rehabilitation protocols. The authors state that cohorts were not controlled for confounders and that athletes with complications may have been lost to follow-up. The pooled 95.3% return rate is not reproducible from the per-study counts (121 of 128 by simple sum), and the McGinnis return rate is given as 94% in the text and 95% in the table. This is a pre-proof version that may change before publication.
practicalImplications : Discuss with the athlete and coach before surgery that the chance of return is high but usually not within the same season, with a mean of about 39 weeks. Surgical choices such as a single-incision approach or suture anchor fixation are associated with differences in return, but the authors say the evidence is not decisive. Early mobilisation may help return time, though this is not yet proven.
athleteDev : Plan the post-repair progression over a full season rather than weeks, because the authors report a mean of about 39 weeks to return. Build elbow flexion and forearm supination strength back in stages, since the review found strength deficits did not clearly change return rates.
rtp : The review reports that about 95% of athletes returned to sport after distal biceps repair, about 82% to the same level, at a mean of about 39 weeks, with a range of 27.6 to 50 weeks. It cannot set clearance criteria or a safe-return timeline for an individual athlete, because the source studies are small, retrospective and use no standard criteria.

29 Distal biceps tendon injuries occur at a rate of 0.9 – 2.55 per 100.000 patients.[1] In the

31 involved in 86% of the cases in the general population.[2] A heavy load on a flexed and supinated
32 forearm can lead to a distal biceps tendon rupture.[3,4] Known risk factors for a distal biceps tendon
33 injury in general, are smoking and steroid abuse.[2] High risk sports for distal biceps tendon ruptures
34 are sports such as: weightlifting, American football, judo and other contact sports.[5]

screeningLimitations : The review draws on four small, mostly retrospective series with different sports, outcomes and rehabilitation protocols, and it reports no confounder adjustment. The pooled return rate cannot be reproduced from the per-study counts, so the evidence cannot set clearance criteria or an individual return timeline.
synthesisCaution : Staff could read the 95% return rate as a likely outcome for any athlete, when it comes from small series, mostly of NFL players and weightlifters, with no comparison group and a possible loss of athletes with complications.
year : 2023
citation : Wörner EA, Nagel M, Kodde IF, Eygendaal D, The B. Return to sports following distal biceps tendon repair: a current concepts review. Journal of ISAKOS 2023 (accepted pre-proof).
doi : 10.1016/j.jisako.2023.02.004
abstract : The article has no abstract in the pre-proof text. Its summary points state that distal biceps tendon repair has a high return-to-sports rate (95%), with 82% returning to the same preinjury level; that functional outcomes are good and not clinically different from matched athletes; that the time to return is long, about 40 weeks; and that the current literature is sparse.
tldr : Most athletes return to sport after distal biceps tendon repair, but usually to the same level only after about 39 weeks, so a return within the same season is unlikely in many sports. The evidence is small and retrospective, so timelines should be set with the athlete and coach.
methods : Narrative review of studies on return to sport after distal biceps tendon repair in athletes. The text does not describe a search strategy, databases, inclusion criteria or appraisal method. The included studies are summarised in a demographics table and a logistic regression table from one study.
findings : Return to sport was 100% (10 of 10) in the weightlifter series, 93.4% (57 of 61) in Gowd et al, 94% (33 of 35) in the NFL series by McGinnis et al (Table 1 gives 95%), and 84% (21 of 22) in Pagani et al. The authors report a mean return time of 6.0 months in Gowd et al and similar NFL performance scores to matched controls, but a shorter career length for defensive backs in Pagani et al. In Gowd et al, a single-incision approach and dominant-side surgery were associated with a longer time to return, and suture anchor fixation with a lower chance of returning at the same or higher level.
limitations : The review has no described search or appraisal, and it relies on four small retrospective studies with different outcomes, sports and rehabilitation protocols. The authors state that cohorts were not controlled for confounders and that athletes with complications may have been lost to follow-up. The pooled 95.3% return rate is not reproducible from the per-study counts (121 of 128 by simple sum), and the McGinnis return rate is given as 94% in the text and 95% in the table. This is a pre-proof version that may change before publication.
practicalImplications : Discuss with the athlete and coach before surgery that the chance of return is high but usually not within the same season, with a mean of about 39 weeks. Surgical choices such as a single-incision approach or suture anchor fixation are associated with differences in return, but the authors say the evidence is not decisive. Early mobilisation may help return time, though this is not yet proven.
athleteDev : Plan the post-repair progression over a full season rather than weeks, because the authors report a mean of about 39 weeks to return. Build elbow flexion and forearm supination strength back in stages, since the review found strength deficits did not clearly change return rates.
rtp : The review reports that about 95% of athletes returned to sport after distal biceps repair, about 82% to the same level, at a mean of about 39 weeks, with a range of 27.6 to 50 weeks. It cannot set clearance criteria or a safe-return timeline for an individual athlete, because the source studies are small, retrospective and use no standard criteria.
